headline: More than 1.5 million people welcome Pope Leo XIV in northern Peru
author: Samantha Schmidt, Anthony Faiola

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering technology with a focus on Tesla, SpaceX and Elon Musk's empire
Musk joins calls for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia

Elon Musk called for the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia on Friday, saying he’d signed a petition for Huang’s reinstatement a day after the chip executive resigned following his admission of an affair with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.
“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk told his more than 240 million followers on X.

It was not immediately clear which petition Musk had signed. Wired reported Thursday that a call for Huang’s return had internally circulated at Nvidia, with more than 1,600 comments — the majority of which supported him coming back.

Huang’s resignation came after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged by some in the intelligence community to be a Chinese spy. Amid the fallout, Huang has garnered vocal support from President Donald Trump and Musk, who has spoken about the irreplaceability of founders and issued other messages backing Huang.
In response to one post suggesting that Musk hire Huang, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO replied: “That would be an honor.”
CHICLAYO, Peru — As the plane touched down in northern Peru, in the adopted home city of the first U.S.-born pope, a local TV station proudly announced: “Pope Leo XIV returns to his land.”

More than 1 million people lined the streets of Chiclayo, Peru, with 500,000 more gathered for a sprawling Friday Mass, according to Vatican estimates, nearly doubling the city’s population for the pope’s emotional homecoming.
“The pope is Chiclayan!” the crowd chanted. “Chiclayo is with you!”

Some in the crowd had been waiting nearly 24 hours for the papal Mass, standing or sitting on the sandy, rock-strewn flat in the scorching sun. Firefighters drove through the vast area spraying the faithful with water.

Yuri Romero, 58, had arrived at 3 p.m. the previous day with her 88-year-old mother. Romero did not sleep, and her arthritic knees ached. But tears filled her eyes as she spoke of her first, and perhaps only, chance to see a pope — a former local bishop who “made you feel like you knew him for a while,” she said.
As the pope passed by and waved at the crowd, a woman holding a Chiclayo flag began to sob. Another held up a bandanna with an image of his home cathedral.
Lenner Mercado, a 39-year-old from Trujillo, and his family drove five hours and walked for three more for the “opportunity to see the Peruvian pope.”
“He was born in the U.S.,” he said, “but his heart is in Peru.”
Reporter covering national politics and breaking news
Brian Monahan out as attending physician to Congress amid Pentagon probe

Rear Adm. Brian Monahan is no longer the attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, more than a year after the Pentagon launched an investigation into alleged misconduct at the office he headed.
“I am no longer serving with the Office of Attending Physicians,” Monahan said in a voicemail message he said had been recorded Wednesday.

Monahan had served since 2009 as the top doctor at the Office of Attending Physician, which provides in-house health care and emergency aid to Congress and the Supreme Court. Within the OAP, Navy medical personnel provide health care under the attending physician’s direction.
Monahan’s departure comes the same week as the Defense Department inspector general’s office published a report that said there had been insufficient oversight of Navy personnel assigned to the OAP.

“Without clinical quality management oversight, Navy personnel may face unclear guidance, inconsistent standards, and pressure to engage in practices that deviate from established medical requirements,” the report stated.

The report also found there had not been the number of regular inspections and inventories of the OAP pharmacy required by law. The most recent inspection, in February, found shortages of sleep aid medication held at the pharmacy versus how many tablets were listed on an inventory, according to the report. There were also discrepancies in the quantities of other controlled substances.

The Navy Times reported Thursday that sailors assigned to the OAP complained of a toxic work environment, including being pressured to work 70 to 80 hours per week and performing unwanted tasks, such as cutting a congressman’s toenails.

Monahan and representatives for the Navy did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday about whether he had been fired or had resigned. The Defense Department referred questions to the Navy.
Meteorologist focused on explaining the atmospheric conditions behind significant weather events
Rare November tornadoes hit Delaware and New Jersey
Severe thunderstorms brought damaging hail and exceptionally rare tornadoes to portions of the Mid-Atlantic on Thursday.

A highly visible and uniquely unobscured tornado tracked southwest of Wilmington, Delaware, near Newark, Delaware. More northeast, another tornado occurred just east of Interstate 95 in Mercer County, New Jersey.

It’s exceptionally rare for tornadoes to happen this time of year in the Mid-Atlantic. It also marked the 115-year anniversary of a damaging F2 tornado that carved through Wilmington on Nov. 12, 1911.

The National Weather Service’s Storm Prediction Center had issued a tornado watch in advance of the storms. A low-pressure system was pulling just enough moisture northward for strong thunderstorms to form, and there was ample wind shear along a warm front. Wind shear describes changing winds with height. Tall storms feel those changing winds and rotate.
Temperatures were rather cool — only around 64 degrees — but it was exceptionally cold aloft. That’s why surface air was still able to rise and produce storms.

Thursday’s storms were supercells, or individual, discrete thunderstorms that were spinning. The Newark, Delaware, tornado occurred around 1 p.m. Radar suggests it was an EF1 on the on the 0-to-5 scale for tornado damage, give or take, with maximum winds around 100 to 110 mph. The weather service will be surveying the damage to make the final call.
Large hail up to the size of golf balls was reported in Burlington and Ocean counties in New Jersey. And in Parkside, Pennsylvania, poor drainage carried hail into piles several feet deep.
Ukraine critic injured in Moscow car bombing, Russia says

A car bombing in Moscow on Friday seriously injured a former adviser to Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov who fled to Russia after his boss’s resignation in 2014 and became a pro-Kremlin commentator.

The explosion came a day after a Russian military officer was killed in a similar attack in St. Petersburg, and it follows a string of assassinations of Russian military figures and high-profile supporters of the war in Ukraine.
According to Russian officials, the car exploded while Sergei Zavorotny, 72, was driving, and he was taken to a hospital in critical condition.

Zavorotny, a former journalist with Komsomolskaya Pravda, served as Azarov’s adviser from 2010 to 2014 and moved to Russia after the ouster of Azarov and President Viktor Yanukovych, who both also fled to Russia. Yanukovich’s decision in late 2013 to abandon an association agreement with the European Union in favor of closer ties with Moscow sparked the Maidan protests.

Since then Zavorotny has been a prominent pro-Russian commentator, who regularly claimed that the Maidan revolution was orchestrated by Western governments. A 2020 U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee report identified him as an officer of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service.

Azarov told Russian state TV he was “shocked” by the attack and accused Ukrainian intelligence services of targeting Zavorotny over his criticism of Ukraine, without providing evidence. Ukrainian officials did not immediately respond to questions about the attack.
National correspondent covering the Southeast
Tanker strikes cruise ship in New Orleans, sending passengers into river

A tanker on Friday afternoon hit a passenger cruise ship that was docked along the Mississippi River in New Orleans, causing a massive emergency response that included firefighters rescuing people from the water.

Kimberly Curth, a Port of New Orleans spokeswoman, said the incident happened at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time when an Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the docked American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage ship that had docked about two hours earlier.
An estimated 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, were aboard the American Heritage at the time, Curth said.

Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel were on scene, conducting rescue and response operations.
Curth said passengers were being brought inside the port’s administration building “for triage and assistance.”

“Our immediate priority is the safety of all passengers, crew members and first responders,” she said in a statement. “This remains an active and evolving incident. The number of injuries and the cause of the collision have not yet been confirmed.”
Reporter covering politics with a focus on campaigns
Van Hollen ‘no longer pursuing’ possible 2028 bid as he seeks Senate leader job
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) is abandoning his presidential ambitions for 2028 as he seeks instead to oust Sen. Chuck Schumer (D) from his leadership role.

“I’m no longer pursuing that,” Van Hollen said Friday of his potential 2028 presidential bid, after a speech to Democrats gathered in Denver to celebrate the party’s huge wins in the midterm elections and chart a cohesive path forward.

“I believe that the size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call of the American people,” Van Hollen said. “We can’t go back to business as usual.”

He announced his challenge to Schumer, the Senate minority leader, late Thursday, sparking a public power struggle alongside the work to unite Democrats. Until this week, Van Hollen had been “kicking the tires” on a presidential bid.
Van Hollen, 67, said the election called for a generational shift and that Schumer, 75, represented a style of politics that voters wanted to change.

He again characterized himself as an underdog in his leadership competition with Schumer, who has led the chamber’s Democratic caucus since 2017. And he declined to publicly reveal how many fellow senators have agreed to support him. But Van Hollen said he spoke directly with Schumer about it.
“We understand that this will be a competition. I think it’s important to give Senate Democrats a choice. That’s what we just gave voters all over the country a choice. They chose change,” he said.
